paper: Lagaris, Likas, Fotiadis (1998) - Artificial Neural Networks for Solving ODEs and PDEs, IEEE TNN 9(5):987-1000 (arXiv physics/9705023 v1)

open_questions.q: How does the exact-BC trial-solution construction Psi_t(x) = A(x) + F(x)*N(x,p) compare, in accuracy and robustness, to modern PINNs' soft-loss boundary-penalty formulation on the SAME set of benchmarks (P1, P3, P5) once the boundary weight lambda is left free?
open_questions.basis: The paper's method enforces BCs exactly by construction (verified in our replication: P1 uses 1+x*N, P3 uses x*sin(1)*e^{-1/5}+x(1-x)*N, P5 uses A(x,y)+x(1-x)y(1-y)*N). Modern PINN literature almost universally uses soft-loss BC penalties instead, citing generality. But no head-to-head A/B on this specific set has been done in our replication, and the trade-off (exact BC + hand-designed A/F vs approximate BC + free-form loss) is a live methodological question. Our REPORT.md, Sec. 6 note 5 flags that hand-designed A(x)/F(x) is why modern PINNs abandoned the approach.
next_steps: Re-implement P1, P3, P5 with a soft-BC PINN loss (residual on interior + boundary MSE * lambda) using the same MLP (1 hidden layer, 10 sigmoid).
Sweep lambda in {1, 10, 100, 1000} and report max_err + RMSE vs the exact-BC trial-solution numbers we already have (2.72e-5, 3.54e-6, 9.59e-7).
Report the boundary-error component separately so 'exact BC' vs 'small BC error' is auditable.

open_questions.q: Does the paper's convergence claim ('1-5 iterations for linear problems' via Merlin BFGS) hold for the trial-solution ANN in a way that is directly comparable to L-BFGS line-search-step counts, or is the claim a solver-specific artefact?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Sec. 6 note 3 and claims-ledger row C8 explicitly note that our L-BFGS ran 594-6250 line-search steps on P1/P3/P5 while the paper cites 1-5 iterations. We flagged this as 'not a discrepancy' (different accounting: Merlin outer iterations vs L-BFGS step counts) but did NOT resolve it. The paper's convergence-guarantee framing therefore has an untested reading.
next_steps: Install Merlin (or a faithful reimplementation of the specific BFGS variant used) and re-run P1, P3, P5 with identical initial weights and grid.
Log outer-iteration count under BOTH definitions (Merlin outer, L-BFGS line-search step) and report side by side.
Cross-reference against convergence theorems for BFGS on the residual functional to say what 'converged' means here (stationary point of sum-of-squares residual, not global minimum).

open_questions.q: How does the trial-solution ANN degrade (or not) on stiff and strongly nonlinear ODE/PDE cases where modern PINNs are known to struggle (e.g., Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Burgers with shock, Allen-Cahn near the transition layer)?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Sec. 8 critique note 7: all five paper worked examples are smooth, low-dimensional, and mostly linear. Our replication inherits this scope. The paper offers no evidence about stiff/nonlinear regimes -- and this is exactly where modern PINN failure modes (spectral bias, loss-landscape pathologies) have been documented. Whether the exact-BC construction helps, hurts, or is irrelevant in stiff regimes is unresolved.
next_steps: Pick a canonical stiff-ODE benchmark (Van der Pol at mu=1000, or Robertson) and a canonical nonlinear-PDE benchmark (viscous Burgers, nu=0.01/pi at T=1).
Implement trial-solution ANN with the same 1x10 sigmoid MLP; report whether it converges to a physically-meaningful solution at all.
Compare against a modern PINN baseline (Adam+L-BFGS, tanh, 4x50) and a classical stiff solver (Radau, IMEX) for grounding.

open_questions.q: Does the trial-solution ANN's error stay comparable to modern PINNs when the dimension is scaled from 2D (P5) to 5D, 10D, or higher, where the boundary-lift construction A(x) becomes combinatorially harder?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Sec. 8 critique note 5: the boundary-lift construction A(x,y) in Eq. 18 is a closed-form bilinear expression on the unit square (verified in our P5 replication with max_err 9.59e-7 on 41x41 grid). In higher dimensions the analytic bilinear/multilinear lift grows exponentially in the number of boundary faces. Whether this remains tractable, and whether the accuracy holds, is not tested by the paper OR our replication.
next_steps: Extend the trial-solution construction to a d-dimensional Poisson problem on the unit hypercube with a known analytic solution for d in {3,5,10}.
Report (a) whether the boundary-lift A(x) can still be written in closed form, (b) how many terms it takes, (c) accuracy at fixed network size, and (d) training time scaling.
Compare against a modern PINN with soft BCs on the same problem to isolate the cost of exact BC enforcement in high d.

open_questions.q: Would adaptive collocation (residual-weighted or importance-sampled) improve the trial-solution ANN's accuracy on P1/P3/P5 relative to the uniform 10-point (ODE) / 10x10 (PDE) grids the paper uses, and by how much?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md Sec. 8 critique note 8: all paper examples use uniform collocation. Modern PINN practice moves toward adaptive collocation because uniform grids over-sample smooth regions. The paper reports max_err ~1e-5 on P1 with 10 uniform points; our replication reproduces this (2.72e-5). Whether adaptive resampling would push these numbers down by 1-2 orders of magnitude at the same total point budget is untested.
next_steps: Implement residual-adaptive resampling on P1: after every 500 L-BFGS steps, replace the K lowest-residual points with K new points sampled by residual magnitude.
Report max_err vs training-step count for uniform vs adaptive at matched total-point budgets (10, 20, 40 points).
Do the same on P5 (2D) with a 10x10 uniform baseline vs adaptive 100-point budget.
